Knowledge graph embeddings (KGE) is a popular method to tackle this problem, which converts entities and relationships into low-dimensional vectors to predict unobserved relationships. However, this approach only employs basic logic to encode available triplets, but struggles to apply universal rules (for example, "all x's wife is x's husband"). Traditional rule-based KG reasoning systems, on the other hand, often depend on rigid rule inference and can be brittle. We introduce RulE, a novel framework that represents and models both logical rules and triplets within a single unified space. By embedding each logical rule and its confidence score, RulE can perform soft rule inference and predict unobserved relationships, similar to KGE's ability to predict unobserved triplets. Unlike KGE alone, RulE allows the integration of logical rules to enhance knowledge graph generalization and the confidence scores of grounded rules to improve rule inference by mitigating logic brittleness. We evaluate our approach with various knowledge graph benchmarks, which demonstrates RulE's superiority on knowledge graph entropy and the accuracy of predicted triples in knowledge graph completion. Furthermore, RulE outperforms KGE alone or with static rules applied after training. We also showcase RulE's ability to provide confident yet sometimes novel and useful predictions on multiple knowledge graph benchmarks. A knowledgeable system operator might choose to disclose relevant information to uninformed users in order to influence them into making more desirable choices. In this study, we examine how public and truthful information-signalling strategies function within Bayesian congestion games on parallel networks. We calculate limits on the benefits that signalling policies can offer, with and without the concurrent use of monetary rewards. We find that while sharing information can reduce system costs in some contexts, it can also lead to poor outcomes, even worse than doing nothing at all. However, using a combination of signalling and incentives allows system operators to ensure that sharing information does not compromise performance while providing equivalent opportunities for improvement. These findings originate from our derived mathematical bounds on the signalling policy's potential benefit. A numerical example illustrates that revealing additional information can negatively impact performance when incentives are absent but can positively affect it when incentives are in place. This counterintuitive phenomenon highlights the significance of considering the dual purposes of signalling policies as both informative and incentive-providing in order to yield optimal system outcomes. Furthermore, our analysis shows that limiting the use of signalling policies to only those that are part of an incentive-sustaining equilibrium maintains system performance and prevents deterioration, thus confirming the reliability of focus on such policies in such scenarios. This study was jointly conducted by researchers at the University of California, Berkeley and the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. "wicked problem," has been a persistent social issue spanning five decades. Research on this complex phenomenon involves diverse spatial, temporal, and social contexts across the globe, with implications for socio-political dynamics throughout history. A crucial area of study within this field seeks to establish reliable predictors of gentrification and/or displacement, with a goal of developing proactive early warning systems. This research builds upon existing scholarship by investigating the essential methodological aspects needed to ensure that these systems can effectively prevent harm and promote justice. Since many relevant PBMs are difficult to solve analytically, researchers often rely on complex numerical methods, like high-order finite difference techniques, to produce reliable solutions, albeit at significant computational costs. A proposed finite difference method leverages operator splitting and calculates each component at its stability threshold to yield nearly negligible discretization errors in some cases, and acceptably low errors in others. Combining specialized mesh design, variable transformations, and exploiting the commutative properties of certain PBMs' differential operators, the new scheme offers considerable efficiency – sometimes down to a mere memory reallocation cost. Clustering algorithms can be evaluated using either internal or external validation metrics. Internal validation metrics evaluate various aspects of partitioned data, but the clusterings they suggest may lack meaning. External validation metrics compare algorithm outputs to expert-provided reference groupings, employing metrics like normalised mutual information or adjusted Rand index. This approach facilitates comparing the clustering of multiple datasets by considering the clustering algorithm's ability to accurately assign entities to known groups. This study aimed to resolve this uncertainty by comparing three data-to-text systems: one that solely utilizes a language model, and two systems enhanced with a data augmentation or pseudo-labeling semi-supervised learning method, respectively.

The results indicate that semi-supervised learning yields superior performance in diversity metrics. Notably, when the training set of a data-to-text system is extended using a pre-trained language model through pseudo-labeling, the output quality scores improve. Conversely, data augmentation results in comparable scores to the system without extended training. Overall, these findings suggest that semi-supervised learning can enhance output quality and diversity, even when augmented with a large-scale language model. 

The code and resources for this study are available on GitHub at https://github.com/dicunxj/data-to-text-ssl. This work has been accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, hosted by the Association for Computational Linguistics.

We addressed this challenge through the use of strain engineering in ordered vertical stacks of SiGe quantum dot pairs. The lower dot in each pair creates favorable conditions for the upper dot to form by exerting strain that also stretches the silicon cap above. The results of these experiments validate the potential of combining active inference and deep learning for navigating complex environments. Resource Allocation (ONRA) plays a vital role in service provisioning. As a sequential problem with uncertain outcomes, it presents a suitable case for tackling via Reinforcement Learning (RL). However, current RL solutions face significant challenges stemming from high sample complexity requirements. To navigate this hurdle, training RL agents in isolation is impractical due to a lack of knowledge about future service demands, while online training in actual networks causes performance deterioration due to temporary sub-optimal policies during prolonged learning periods. This degradation is particularly pronounced in non-stationary ONRA scenarios, where adapting to shifting service requirements is crucial. To circumvent this problem, a model-based resource allocation framework called RADAR is proposed, designed for ONRA applications with immediately known action rewards. By strategically balancing exploration of the state space in the background with real-time policy exploitation, leveraging synthetic data generated from the trained background model, RADAR effectively boosts sample efficiency. When applied to a multi-domain service federation problem to maximize profits by selecting suitable domains for service request placement, RADAR showcases its ability to adapt continuously and achieves notable performance gains, specifically up to a 44% improvement over standard RL models without prior knowledge. Furthermore, the extensive evaluation shows that RADAR achieves robustness by reducing performance drops in comparison to traditional RL models across diverse scenarios. This model's ability to adapt and learn simultaneously in the background and real-time facilitates its extensive potential applications in various real-world ONRA scenarios with shifting requirements. our investigation focuses on how much information a guessing adversary can gain. The underlying source coding problem is represented by a confusion graph, illustrating how source symbols can be distinguished from one another. The adversary's ability to successfully guess the source sequence is measured relative to its prior knowledge, with this measurement maximized over various source distributions. When the adversary follows a specific model where they only make a single guess and can perfectly match their guess to the true sequence, this measurement is known as the maximal leakage in literature and can be expressed as the maximum min-entropy leakage. We establish a comprehensive single-letter representation of the optimal normalized leakage in this adversarial scenario, along with a stochastic coding method that reaches this optimum. Interestingly, our analysis shows that both the optimal leakage and optimal compression rates are attainable by certain deterministic coding strategies, where these goals can be concurrently achieved. We expand upon the initial investigation to consider adversaries that submit multiple guesses and can tolerate a degree of sequence error. In this case, we identify tight lower and upper bounds for the more general leakage metric through the application of single-letter analysis. Additionally, we demonstrate that these bounds can be tightly represented by a deterministic coding method. Lastly, our study delves into the consideration of adversaries that only make a single guess but with a more relaxed matching criterion, resulting in a modified leakage metric. Here as well, we apply single-letter analysis to provide tight lower and upper bounds for this metric, showing that they can be closely represented by a deterministic coding method.
